DICOM: the Information Model, Objects, Services, and the Conformance Statement

Unit 1: Imaging Informatics Foundations. Lesson 2 of 65 in CIIP Academy.

A vendor promises their new ultrasound scanner "speaks DICOM." Your job is to find out exactly what that means before the purchase order is signed, because DICOM is a family of choices, not a single switch.

The information model

DICOM organizes data as patient, then study, then series, then instance. One patient has many studies, a study has many series, and a series has many instances such as images. Each level carries a UID, a globally unique dotted number of up to 64 characters built on a root the organization owns. Two different objects must never share a UID.

Objects, services, and roles

A SOP class pairs a service with an object type, such as CT image storage. A SOP instance is one object of that class. In every exchange one side is the service class user (it asks) and the other the service class provider (it answers). A modality storing to PACS is the user; PACS is the provider.

The association

Two devices open an association: the requester proposes presentation contexts (a SOP class plus the transfer syntaxes it can use), the other side accepts or rejects each one, data flows, then the association is released.

The core services

C-ECHO tests the connection, C-STORE sends an object, C-FIND queries, C-MOVE asks a provider to send matches to a named destination, and C-GET retrieves over the same association. DICOMweb offers store, query, and retrieve over HTTP.

The header and tags

Every DICOM object carries a header of data elements, each addressed by a tag written as (group,element). A few matter every day: (0010,0010) is the patient name, (0010,0020) is the patient ID, (0008,0050) is the accession number that ties the images to the order, and (0020,000D) is the study instance UID. When a study will not match, read these four first.

Reading the conformance statement

Every product ships one. It lists the SOP classes, user and provider roles, transfer syntaxes, and options. Read it before buying.

Exam tip: when two devices cannot exchange something, compare their conformance statements for the SOP class, the role, and a shared transfer syntax. Unique UIDs are the rule that keeps studies from colliding.
Remember
DICOM is patient, study, series, and instance with a unique UID at each level, services negotiated in an association, and a conformance statement that tells you what a product really supports.
Deeper explanation

DICOM: the Information Model, Objects, Services, and the Conformance Statement, explained slowly

Reading a DICOM header

Every DICOM file is a set of data elements, each addressed by a tag written as (group,element). Knowing a handful of tags lets you read a header dump and find why a study will not match.

Tag             Attribute                 Used for
(0010,0010)     Patient's name            display, matching
(0010,0020)     Patient ID                matching to the master patient record
(0008,0050)     Accession number          ties images to the order
(0008,0060)     Modality                  protocol selection, routing
(0020,000D)     Study instance UID        names the study, never reused
(0020,000E)     Series instance UID       names the series
(0008,0018)     SOP instance UID          names one image
(0028,0010)     Rows                      matrix height
(0028,0011)     Columns                   matrix width
(0028,0100)     Bits allocated            storage per pixel

An association, step by step

A CT scanner stores a slice to PACS.

  1. The scanner (the user) opens a connection to the PACS address and port and proposes an association, naming its own AE title and the PACS AE title.
  2. In the request it lists presentation contexts: CT image storage, offered with explicit little endian and JPEG lossless.
  3. PACS (the provider) checks the calling AE title against its allowed list. If the title is unknown it rejects the association here.
  4. PACS accepts the context and picks one transfer syntax, say explicit little endian.
  5. The scanner sends the slice. PACS answers with a status: success, or a warning or failure code.
  6. The scanner releases the association.

What the walk-through diagnoses

Rejected at step 3 means an AE title problem. Accepted but a context refused at step 4 means no shared SOP class or syntax. Failure status at step 5 means PACS could not store, for example because the disk is full or because a UID clashed with another object.

Worked UID example

A hospital owns the root 1.2.3.4. It builds each study UID from the root plus a device number, a date, and a counter, for example 1.2.3.4.5.20261123.17. The UID may be at most 64 characters, so a long root leaves little room, which is why roots are kept short.
